pr_title: Add an option to do zero byte reads on StreamPipeReader
pr_body:
- Added UseZeroByteReads to StreamPipeReader options that allows not allocating a buffer by doing a zero byte read on the underlying Stream before the internal buffer is allocated.

Fixes #37539

issue_context.title: Add ability to perform zero byte reads in StreamPipeReader
issue_context.body:
## Background and Motivation

Bufferless reads are a technique used in a couple of places in ASP.NET Core to avoid renting memory from the memory pool if there's no data available on the socket; this helps when trying to reduce the memory usage for idle connections for applications that are trying to handle a large number of concurrent connections (like websocket based applications).

We'd like to use this for websocket applications to remove the need to allocate any memory (see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/37122 for an example)

<!--
We welcome API proposals! We have a process to evaluate the value and shape of new API. There is an overview of our process [here](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/project/api-review-process.md). This template will help us gather the information we need to start the review process.
First, please describe the purpose and value of the new API here.
-->

## Proposed API

```diff
namespace System.Collections.Generic
{
    public class StreamPipeReaderOptions 
    {
+      public bool WaitForData { get; set; }
    }
```


WaitForData tells the PipeReader implementation that it should wait for data from the underlying stream before allocating memory. It relies on the stream supporting zero byte reads (which networking and SSL do)

## Usage Examples

``` C#
var reader = PipeReader.Create(stream, new StreamPipeReaderOptions { WaitForData = true })
```

## Numbers in SSLStream

- During TLS Handshakes we allocate an 8K buffer while waiting for the handshake
- During pending TLS reads we allocate a 16K buffer per read
    - The caller then allocates a 4K buffer on top of this so we burn 20K per connection in pooled buffers (that shouldn't be pooled, see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/49001)
comments:
For reference, here's the snippet [from MSDN](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.stream.read):

> Read returns 0 only when there is no more data in the stream and no more is expected (such as a closed socket or end of file).

The contrapositive to this statement is "if there might be more data in the stream, `Read` returns a non-zero value." Combined with that `Read` cannot return a negative value and that it cannot return a value greater than the number of bytes requested, the only logical conclusion is that it's a contract violation (per the docs) to pass a zero-length buffer in to the `Read` method. However, since implementations may or may not be checking for zero-length inputs, what this really means is that the behavior is undefined / implementation-dependent.

Please don't couple the 2 APIs together. If the wrapping Stream doesn't support zero byte reads then it should throw (or return 0 I guess?). When it does though, like SSLStream and NetworkStream, this passthrough should just work (they are verified and have tests)

> Please don't couple the 2 APIs together. If the wrapping Stream doesn't support zero byte reads then it should throw (or return 0 I guess?). When it does though, like SSLStream and NetworkStream, this passthrough should just work (they are verified and have tests)

What we heard was that it was not critical for Kestrel in 5.0, so a foolproof end-to-end usage is better. If critical, we can accept the API separately and demand good documentation that it expects non-standard Stream behavior.

It's not critical for Kestrel in 5.0 but that's not the point of this API. I don't mind adding the API to stream either but the purity argument being made doesn't change the API on StreamPipeReader, nor does it change what happens if the underlying Stream doesn't support it. This API is .NET Standard 2.0 so it runs in all the places (where there won't be a new WaitForDataAsync API). 

For all you know, the StreamPipeReader could implement this by doing a big switch statement on the stream type and determine which ones support zero byte reads and throw if that isn't the case.

I'd like the 2 APIs decoupled in general because they don't need overlap.
